title: Ibn Tulun's mosque
hook: an old Cairo mosque with a spiral minaret

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Azhar in Cairo: a mosque where classes met in rings beside the pillars. Your line was: a thousand years of study. Did you give fifteen minutes to learning something properly? Day nine hundred forty-eight.

Build the minaret like this. The man saying it is holding up a strip of paper he has been idly rolling around his finger during a meeting, now a tight coil. That's a story told about Ahmad ibn Tulun, who governed Egypt in the name of the Abbasid caliphs before Cairo itself existed. It may not be true. But walk around his mosque today and the minaret does look a little like that coil: a stair wrapped around the outside of the tower, climbing as it turns. Today: Ibn Tulun's mosque.
screen: `A STRIP OF PAPER, ROLLED UP.` → `BUILD THE MINARET LIKE THIS.` → `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.`

segments.voice: Start with the big picture. Ibn Tulun built in his own capital, a settlement just south of where the Fatimids would later lay out Cairo. Over time the city grew around his mosque, and so it now stands inside Cairo, older than the city around it. Step through the gate and the first thing is space: a huge open courtyard, plain arcades of pointed arches on every side, and a fountain in the middle for washing before prayer. Some visitors say the plainness is the point. Nothing much to look at except light, shadow and the next arch. Then the stair. This minaret doesn't hide its steps inside. It puts them outside, so anyone looking up can see the path the caller to prayer would climb, turning and rising. Historians link the shape to the great spiral minaret at Samarra, the Abbasid capital where, tradition says, Ibn Tulun grew up. So the paper story and the Samarra story might both be explaining the same thing: why a mosque in Egypt has a stair that winds around the outside. A turning stair is also a good picture of remembrance, dhikr. You go around, and around, and every turn looks almost like the last, but you are higher each time. The Qur'an says it this way, in Pickthall's translation: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" In that picture, repeating the same words, the same prayers, the same small acts, isn't walking in a circle. It's climbing. The spiral stair.
screen: `OLDER THAN THE CITY AROUND IT.` · `A COURTYARD OF LIGHT AND ARCHES.` · `A STAIR ON THE OUTSIDE.` · `EVERY TURN A LITTLE HIGHER.` · then, large: `IN THE REMEMBRANCE OF ALLAH DO HEARTS FIND REST.`

segments.voice: The practice: climb slowly, in remembrance. If there are stairs near you, walk up them as slowly as you can, one step at a time, for the length of the sit. If there aren't, stand, or sit, and slowly turn your attention in a circle: breath in, breath out, and again. If you pray, you can say a word of dhikr with each step, such as Subhan Allah, glory be to God. If you don't, count each step, or each breath. Notice that every turn feels the same, and that you are not where you started. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Tulun. The governor of Egypt whose mosque, now inside Cairo, has a wide courtyard and a minaret whose stair winds around the outside. Today's word.
Your line: the spiral stair. Today, when something you repeat every day starts to feel like going in circles, take it one step slower, and notice where it's taking you. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: The mosque of Ibn Tulun still stands in Cairo, and visitors can climb the stair on the outside of its minaret. Dhikr is practiced by repeating short phrases such as Subhan Allah.
